clinicalPearls: A progressive, constricting fibrous band that forms at the base of a digit, most characteristically the fifth toe, eventually causing spontaneous autoamputation
Predominantly seen in adults of African and other tropical-region descent, often in those who habitually walk barefoot
Progresses through stages from a painful constricting groove to bulbous swelling of the distal digit, bone resorption and finally spontaneous separation
Termed 'true ainhum' when idiopathic, distinguished from 'pseudo-ainhum' where a similar constricting band arises secondary to another condition
Radiographs show soft-tissue constriction with progressive tapering and osteolysis of the underlying phalanx
Pseudo-ainhum should prompt a search for underlying causes such as scleroderma, leprosy, psoriasis, keratoderma or diabetic/neuropathic disease
Management ranges from Z-plasty release of the constricting band early on to surgical amputation once the digit is non-viable
reference.pathophysiology: Ainhum is a slowly progressive constricting fibrotic process affecting a digit, classically the fifth toe. A hyperkeratotic groove develops and deepens into a circumferential fibrous band that progressively strangulates the soft tissues, impairing local blood flow and lymphatic drainage. The resulting distal congestion causes bulbous swelling, while chronic ischaemia and pressure drive progressive resorption of the underlying phalangeal bone, culminating in spontaneous autoamputation. The idiopathic 'true' form has been linked to chronic trauma from barefoot walking and possibly vascular insufficiency, whereas 'pseudo-ainhum' represents an identical constricting band occurring secondary to systemic or dermatological disease that must be identified.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudo-ainhum secondary to scleroderma or systemic sclerosis
Psoriasis or hereditary keratoderma with constricting bands
Peripheral vascular disease with digital ischaemia
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs of the digit showing soft-tissue constriction and progressive phalangeal osteolysis
Clinical examination to stage the constricting band and assess distal viability
Screening for secondary causes (scleroderma serology, leprosy assessment, skin examination for keratoderma)
Assessment of peripheral circulation and neuropathy
Biopsy of the band in atypical cases to exclude other pathology
redFlags: Signs of secondary infection or gangrene in the constricted digit
Rapid progression or features suggesting an underlying systemic disease (pseudo-ainhum)
Multiple or atypically distributed digits involved
reference.prognosis: True ainhum is slowly progressive and, if untreated, leads over years to spontaneous autoamputation of the affected digit; early band release can preserve the digit, and outcome in pseudo-ainhum depends on the underlying disease.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish pseudo-ainhum and therefore missing a treatable underlying systemic disease
Delaying surgical band release until the digit is already non-viable
Overlooking secondary infection in the constricted, congested digit
Attributing the lesion to trauma alone without appropriate imaging and screening
management: Early surgical release of the constricting band with Z-plasty to interrupt the fibrous ring and preserve the digit
Topical keratolytics and emollients to soften the hyperkeratotic groove in early disease
Amputation of the digit when autoamputation is imminent or the distal part is non-viable or infected
Identify and treat pseudo-ainhum by managing the underlying disorder such as scleroderma, leprosy, psoriasis, keratoderma or neuropathy
Footwear advice and foot protection to reduce chronic trauma from barefoot walking
Wound care and prevention of secondary infection of the strangulated digit
Regular review to stage band progression and assess distal viability and circulation
